prose.summary: Product designers shape how a digital product works, not only how it looks. They connect user research, interaction design, prototypes and design systems to product decisions. The role overlaps heavily with UX design but often carries broader ownership from problem through shipped interface.
prose.day_to_day: The work moves between flows, prototypes, critiques, design-system components and conversations with product and engineering. Designers test assumptions, resolve edge cases and adjust work when technical constraints become clear. Current titles lean senior and span enterprise, authentication, education and AI products. The output is a usable product behavior with a reason behind it.
prose.work_environment: The live openings include substantial remote work alongside hybrid and office roles across several countries. Collaboration remains constant because design decisions depend on engineering feasibility, product priority and user evidence. Senior hiring dominates the visible sample, which raises the bar for portfolio ownership.
prose.getting_in: Build a portfolio around complete product decisions rather than isolated screens. Show the problem, research or evidence, alternatives, prototype, constraints and what changed after testing. UX designers have the closest measured route, while visual or brand designers need stronger interaction and product evidence.
prose.ladder: Early designers own contained flows and components. Responsibility grows toward product areas, design systems, strategy and mentoring across teams. The path can branch into UX research, design technology, creative direction or product leadership.
prose.suits: This work suits people who enjoy visual craft but accept that constraints and user evidence can overturn a preferred solution. It requires comfort with critique, unfinished questions and detailed edge cases. It is a poor fit if polished screens matter more than product behavior.
prose.misconceptions: Product design is not a prettier name for graphic design. The measured routes emphasize interaction, prototyping, systems, research and product judgment alongside visual work.
prose.who_qualifies: UX designers, design technologists, researchers and interaction-focused visual designers bring adjacent foundations. The transition needs a case study showing shipped behavior and tradeoffs. A gallery of static screens leaves too much unanswered.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: Listings cannot show whether designers influence product strategy or mainly decorate requirements set elsewhere. That authority changes the job more than a senior title does.

steps.how: Work on a real flow with users, constraints and failure cases rather than inventing a cosmetic redesign.
Use Figma or another tool to test sequence, states and edge cases before polishing the surface.
Run focused research or usability testing and show which design decision changed because of it.
Explain technical constraints, rejected directions and the final product rationale in a concise case study.

prose.tools: The route evidence centers on Figma, prototyping, interaction design, design systems, wireframing, research, usability testing and accessibility. Visual design matters, but the portfolio must connect those tools to product behavior.

industries.name: Consumer software
industries.note: Designers optimize frequent journeys, discovery and retention-sensitive interactions.

industries.name: Enterprise products
industries.note: Work handles dense workflows, permissions and users with specialized tasks.

industries.name: Identity and security
industries.note: Design decisions must make safety and account controls understandable.

industries.name: AI products
industries.note: Interfaces need to communicate uncertain output, correction and user control.

specializations.name: Interaction design
specializations.why: It focuses on flows, states and how users act through the product.

specializations.name: Design systems
specializations.why: It creates reusable patterns that keep many product surfaces coherent.

specializations.name: Enterprise product design
specializations.why: It addresses complex workflows, roles and information density.

pros: The work combines user evidence, systems thinking and visual craft.
Product experience transfers across industries and adjacent design roles.
cons: Senior portfolios face a high bar in the current openings.
Design authority can be narrow even when the title sounds broad.

faq.q: how do you become a product designer?
faq.a: Build case studies that show a product problem, user evidence, interaction choices and technical tradeoffs through to a usable outcome. Static visual work is not enough.

faq.q: can a UX designer become a product designer?
faq.a: Yes. The measured overlap is very strong, and the main addition is often broader ownership of product strategy, systems and delivery.

faq.q: what is the difference between product design and UX design?
faq.a: Product design often covers UX, visual systems and product ownership across delivery, while UX design may focus more tightly on research and interaction. Company practice matters more than the title.
